                 ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY'S COMMENTS
              ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.521

           Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC ("Oncof') files these comments in response to the

Public Utility Commission of Texas's (the "Commission") proposal for publication of 16 Tex.

Admin. Code ("TAC") §25.521 issued in this rulemaking proceeding on July 30,2026. Refer to

Attachment 1 for a redline version of the proposed rule. Oncor appreciates the opportunity to

assist with Staff's efforts to implement Senate Bill 6 and emerging Texas policy for large loads.

           Oncor's principal recommendation is that the new rule authorize the Electric Reliability

Council of Texas, Inc. ("ERCOT") to procure and deploy Large Load Demand Management

Service ("LLDMS") for anticipated or actual transmission emergencies, not only for energy

emergency alert events caused by extreme weather. The proposal defines "transmission

emergency" but never uses the term, and Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PURA") § 39.170(b)

does not limit the service that narrowly. ERCOT agreed with this reading in its April 8, 2026

comments in this docket. 1 Oncor's remaining comments address the order of operations for

deployment under PURA § 37.0561(e), Security Constrained Economic Dispatch ("SCED") of

loads subject to PURA § 39.170(a), and several conforming and technical corrections.


   I.      ONCOR'S RESPONSES TO ENUMERATED OUESTIONS FOR COMMENT




           1 Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc.'s Response to Commission Staff's List of Questions at 2-3 (Apr.
8,2026).

     1. Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity

       representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is

       subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management

       Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available

       but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be

       compensated some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load

       customer's availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If

       so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load customer for their availability

       during the LLDMS obligation period?

       Oncor elects not to respond to Question No. 1. Oncor notes only that the rule should state

where LLDMS deployment falls in the order of operations relative to the threshold ERCOT must

establish under PURA § 37.0561(e). LLDMS should be deployed before that threshold is crossed,

not after. The two provisions also carry different pricing consequences. PURA § 37.0561(e)

requires ERCOT to treat a deployment under that provision as firm load shed when calculating

price adjustments for reliability deployments, while PURA § 39.170(c) requires only that an

LLDMS deployment be included in that calculation. Oncor's proposed modification to subsection

(i), shown in Attachment 1, directs ERCOT to address this sequencing and the resulting price

adjustments in its protocols.

   2. Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar

       year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       Oncor elects not to respond to Question No. 2. Oncor notes only that its recommendation

to extend LLDMS to transmission emergencies, described in its response to Question No. 4 below,

does not require an increase to the program budget. Because LLDMS is procured on an as-needed

ONCOR'S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION'S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.521                                                                             Page 2 of 11

                                                                                                2
 basis, extending the conditions under which ERCOT may procure the service does not obligate

ERCOT to procure more of it.


   3. What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how

       far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

       Oncor recommends that the rule should establish three parameters:

       •   The LLDMS procurement period should be short. A procured large load customer takes

           operational steps in reliance on its commitment, and an extended procurement period

           could increase the cost and risk of participation without a corresponding reliability

           benefit. Oncor recommends a procurement period of no more than seven days ahead of

           a forecasted need.

       •   ERCOT should be permitted to procure in stages. ERCOT should be able to issue an

           initial request for proposal approximately seven days ahead of a forecasted need and,

           if its forecast indicates that additional capacity may be required, issue additional

           requests as needed. Staged procurement allows ERCOT to align the procured quantity

           with forecasted needs rather than committing to a single quantity at the outset.

       •   The rule should confirm that procured capacity is entitled to payment, subject only to

           the availability and performance adjustments in subsections (f)(1) and (g). Participants

           will incur costs upon award, and payment certainty is necessary to attract participation.

   For these reasons, §§ 25.521(d)(1), and (f) should be modified to limit the length of the

LLDMS procurement period, authorize staggered procurement in advance of a forecasted need,

and confirm that procured capacity is entitled to payment.

   4. Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,

       what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

§25.521                                                                                Page 3 of 11

         Yes. The Commission should not impose limitations on its LLDMS authority. Participation

in LLDMS is voluntary, and deployment should remain fully within ERCOT's operational

discretion as provided for by ERCOT protocols developed for that purpose. Extending the

conditions under which ERCOT may procure LLDMS does not obligate ERCOT to procure more

of it, it simply provides ERCOT more operational flexibility. Oncor submits that LLDMS service

could be deployed selectively and not system wide which will allow for procurement to be

followed by selective deployment to efficiently address a regional or localized transmission

emergency. Regional and localized emergency conditions can have substantial reliability impacts

including the possibility of cascading into system-wide emergency conditions if not mitigated

quickly. ERCOT should be able to rely on LLDMS to address each ofthese types of emergencies.2

If the Commission adopts Oncor's recommendation to allow ERCOT to deploy LLDMS for

transmission emergencies, Oncor posits that ERCOT should develop protocols which will control

the procurement and deployment of LLDMS for transmission emergencies.

        The definition of "transmission emergency" in subsection (b)(4) should be modified to

reach a condition in which a transmission element is operating, or is forecasted to operate, above

its emergency rating, so that the definition supports the advance procurement authority it is

intended to enable.        Oncor thus proposes modifications to proposed §§ 25.521(b)(4), (d),

(d)(1)(C)-(D),(e)(2), and (e)(3)(A) to implement this change, as shown in Attachment 1 to these

comments.

        PURA § 39.170(b) does not limit LLDMS to energy emergency alert events caused by

extreme weather. The statute directs the Commission to require a reliability service to be deployed

at 2-3,5 (Apr. 8,2026).

 "in the event of an anticipated emergency condition." ERCOT reached the same conclusion in this

proj ect, stating in its April 8 comments: 3

         "As noted, PURA § 39.170(b) explicitly states the Commission must require ERCOT to
         develop a reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency
         condition. Notably, this language does not say that the service is to be deployed in the event
         of an 'anticipated extreme weather event.' However, PURA § 39.170(b) then specifies
         several requirements for the Commission's rule, including a requirement to specify the
         periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during 'extreme
         weather events.' Therefore, ERCOT believes that a plain language reading of the statute
         gives the Commission authority to draft a broader rule to address circumstances that are
         unrelated to an extreme weather event, including an anticipated EEA event, transmission
         emergency, or other emergency condition that may not be associated with extreme
         weather."
         The Independent Market Monitor likewise recommended in its comments in this docket

that the service be available during any event presenting a material risk of firm load shed,

regardless of whether the event is weather-driven. 4 ERCOT has taken the same position in the net

metering rulemaking, telling the Commission that an "Emergency Condition" includes "either a

system capacity emergency (Energy Emergency Alert [EEAI) or a transmission emergency."5

         To the extent the Commission is concerned that the 24-hour notice requirement in

subsection (e)(1) and the obligation to remain deployed under subsection (e)(3) do not suit a

transmission emergency, two modifications resolve that concern. First, the rule should confirm that

ERCOT may issue the 24-hour notice when it determines an emergency condition is probable,

without committing to deploy, and may withdraw the notice. Second, subsection (e)(3)(A) should




          3 Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc.'s Response to Commission Staff's List of Questions at 2-3 (Apr.
8,2026). Oncor acknowledges ERCOT's observation that transmission emergencies and non-storm EEA events "are
less likely to occur with as much notice" as a winter storm. Id. at 3. ERCOT made that observation, however, in
explaining why a seasonal procurement structure would give it greater flexibility to address those events. Shorter
notice is a reason to give ERCOT procurement authority in advance of a forecasted transmission emergency, not a
reason to withhold deployment authority once capacity is in place.

 require a deployed customer to remain deployed for the duration ofthe EEA event or transmission

emergency. Together these give ERCOT the flexibility to position capacity in advance of a

forecasted transmission emergency without obligating deployment.

        Transmission emergencies can be forecasted. ERCOT issues notices of anticipated

transmission emergencies today, based on conditions including low wind forecasts and extreme

winter weather, and does so without electing whether to procure or deploy any service. The

recently announced west Texas Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits (IROLs) are a good

example of how transmission emergencies can be anticipated.6 In that context, ERCOT was

monitoring two import constraints whose limits must be treated as IROLs requiring action up to

pre-contingency load shed to prevent them from being exceeded and prevent the risk of

widespread, uncontrolled outages. The driver for these circumstances was a known weather-

related emergency. During extended low wind conditions at night, the imports to the load in the

area, offset by the flows from the remaining Resources, may overload the thermal capacity of

individual transmission lines.

                  II.    ONCOR'S COMMENTS ON NEW 16 TAC %25.521

    1. § 25.521(a)(1) - This subsection should be modified to require that the electric

        cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility

        subject to it confer with customers to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated

        manner and be dispatchable through the SCED process, because a transmission

        service provider ("TSP") cannot enforce a partial curtailment at a customer's site.




        6 See ERCOT Board of Directors Meeting , Item 13 , Far West Load Growth and Transmission Timing Issues
(Feb. 9-10, 2026) (accessible at https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/02/04/13-Far-West-Load-Growth-and-
Transmission-Timing-Issues.pdf).

         Subsection (a)(1) should be conformed to the full text of PURA § 39.170(a). The proposed

rule omits the statute's directive that the electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility,

or municipally owned utility confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a

coordinated manner. To that end, subsection (a)(1) should further require that a load subject to it

register with ERCOT and install remote systems that allow the load to be dispatched or controlled

through the security-constrained economic dispatch process. As Oncor explained in its April 8,

2026 comments, a TSP can open or hold the breaker at a large load site but cannot enforce a partial

curtailment. Complete disconnection eliminates the partial curtailment LLDMS contemplates, and

it would disconnect any backup generation or co-located generation resource made available to the

ERCOT grid under PURA § 39.169(d). Centralized SCED dispatch, delivered through qualified

scheduling entity ("QSE"), is the only practical means of accomplishing the curtailment PURA §

39.170(a) requires. Centralized SCED dispatch is also warranted to allow utilities the ability to

operate their systems to best address challenges associated with today's more complex system,

which is constantly evolving and changing. In designing LLDMS and enabling centralized SCED

dispatch through a requirement in this rule, utilities will be enabled to meet and address such issues,

including transmission emergencies that may be coming down the line.

    2. § 25.521(c)(2) - This subsection should be modified so that ineligibility attaches to

        committed curtailable capacity rather than to the large load customer, to supply a

       verification mechanism for subparagraph (D), and to add registration as a Load

        Resource, including a Provisional Controllable Load Resource to the enumerated list.


        As Oncor explained in its April 8,2026 comments, the rule should not disqualify an entire

large load customer from LLDMS because a portion of its capacity is committed to another service.

The lead-in to subsection (c)(2) should be modified so that ineligibility attaches to the committed

ONCOR'S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION'S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.521                                                                                   Page 7 of 11

                                                                                                      7
 curtailable capacity rather than to the customer, and a large load customer should be permitted to

offer the remaining, uncommitted portion of its load. ERCOT needs assurance that the capacity it

procures will be available when called upon; it does not need to exclude the customer entirely.

         The enumerated list should also include participation as a Load Resource, including a

Provisional Controllable Load Resource. Capacity available for dispatch as a Load Resource

should not also be offered as LLDMS.

         Subparagraph (D) requires a verification mechanism. As drafted, the prohibition on

participation by a customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity provides

no means of enforcement. Oncor recommends that the rule require a QSE to attest, on behalf of

each large load customer it represents, that the offered capacity is not committed to or obligated

under any service or program listed in subsection (c)(2).

    3. § 25.521(f)(3), (g)(1), and (h) - These subsections should be modified to correct an

         undefined cost-allocation period, supply the omitted reinstatement criteria for a

         qualified scheduling entity, and align the after-action reporting requirement with the

         events that trigger it.

         The following modifications to subsections (f)(3), (g)(1), and (h) correct internal

inconsistencies in the proposed rule and align it with the Commission's existing reliability service

rules.

         Subsection (f)(3) allocates LLDMS deployment costs to each load serving entity based on

its load ratio share "during the procurement period." That term is not defined in the rule. The

Commission's fiscal note describes the same charge as based on load ratio share during the relevant

LLDMS obligation period, which is a defined term in subsection (b)(3). Subsection (f)(3) should

be conformed to use the defined term.

ONCOR'S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION'S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.521                                                                                Page 8 of 11

                                                                                                   8
         Subsection (f)(3) also reaches only deployment costs, while the budget cap in subsection

(f)(4) is expressed in terms of procurement costs. The rule does not state how the availability

payments authorized by subsection (f)(1)(C) are recovered. The Commission's firm fuel supply

service rule addresses this distinction expressly, and § 25.521 should do the same.

        Subsection (g)(1) should require ERCOT to establish criteria for reinstatement of a

suspended QSE. Subsection (g)(2) requires reinstatement criteria for a suspended large load

customer, and both the emergency response service rule and the firm fuel supply service rule

require reinstatement criteria for a QSE. The omission from (g)(1) appears inadvertent.

        Subsection (h) requires an after-action report following "an event in which ERCOT

procures LLDMS." The reporting elements addressing duration of deployment and performance

during deployment are qualified as applicable, which suggests the requirement is intended to

capture deployments as well. Subsection (h) should be modified to require a report following an

event in which ERCOT procures or deploys LLDMS. If the Commission adopts Oncor's

recommendation regarding transmission emergencies, the report should also identify the type of

emergency condition that prompted the procurement or deployment and the location of the

procured and deployed capacity.

                                   III.   CONCLUSION

       Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff's efforts to amend the Commission's

rules pursuant to Senate Bill 6.

     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY'S COMMENTS ON THE
       COMMISSION'S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.521
•    Oncor does not take a position on whether a large load customer that is available but not
     deployed should be compensated, but notes that the rule should specify where LLDMS
     deployment falls in the order of operations relative to the curtailment threshold ERCOT must
     establish under PURA § 37.0561(e)

•    Oncor does not take a position on the appropriate LLDMS budget, and notes that extending
     LLDMS to transmission emergencies does not require an increase to it because the service is
     procured on an as-needed basis.

•    Oncor recommends a procurement period of no more than seven days ahead of a forecasted
     need, staged procurement in advance of a forecasted need, and confirmation that procured
     capacity is entitled to payment.

•    ERCOT should be able to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies, which can be
     forecasted and which can cascade into system-wide emergency conditions if not mitigated
     quickly, and the Commission should not limit that authority because participation is voluntary
     and deployment should remain within ERCOT's operational discretion.

•    Subsections (b)(4), (d), (d)(1)(C)-(D), (e)(2), and (e)(3)(A) should be modified to authorize
     ERCOT to procure and deploy LLDMS for an anticipated or actual transmission emergency.

•    Subsection (a)(1) should be conformed to the full text of PURA § 39.170(a) and should
     implement the statute's directive that the electric cooperative, transmission and distribution
     utility, or municipally owned utility confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load
     in a coordinated manner. Further, the rule should require that loads subj ect to it register with
     ERCOT and be dispatchable through SCED, because a TSP cannot enforce a partial curtailment
     at a customer's site.

•    Subsection (c)(1) should be modified so that ineligibility attaches to committed curtailable
     capacity rather than to the large load customer, and should include a verification mechanism
     for subparagraph (D).

•    Subsections (f)(3), (g)(1), and (h) should be modified to correct an undefined cost-allocation
     period, supply the omitted reinstatement criteria for a qualified scheduling entity, and align the
     after-action reporting requirement with the events that trigger it.

•    Subsection (i) should be modified to direct ERCOT to establish, in its protocols, a clear order
     of operations for LLDMS deployment relative to the PURA § 37.0561(e) threshold and how
     each deployment is reflected in price adjustments for reliability deployments.

 §25.521. Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS).

(a)   Directive to ERCOT.

      (l)     ERCOT must ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution
              utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-voltage customer
              develops a protocol, including the installation of any necessary equipment or
              technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed
              during firm load shed via Security Constrained Economic Dispatch. The electric
              cooperative, transmission and distribution utility. or municipallv owned utility shall
              confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner.
              This subsection applies to a load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is
              not:

              (A)     load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined by Public
                      Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §17.002; or

              (B)     designated as a critical natural gas facility under PURA §38.074.

      (2)     ERCOT must develop a Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS) to
              competitively procure demand reductions from large load customers consistent
              with this section.

(b)   Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the following
      meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:

      (1)     Extreme weather condition -- A weather condition that creates a significant risk
              for an energy emergency alert (EEA) event.

      (2)     Large load customer -- An entity with a total non-coincident peak demand at a
              single site that is equal to or greater than 75 megawatts (MW).

      (3)     LLDMS obligation period -- The period identified in a LLDMS agreement
              through which a procured large load customer is obligated to provide LLDMS.

      (4)     Transmission emergency -- A condition in which an element on the transmission
              system is operating above its emergency rating, or is forecasted to operate above
              its emergency rating such that it creates a significant risk of firm load shed.

(c)   Participation. Participation in LLDMS is limited to large load customers that pre-qualify
      for participation at least annually.

      (1)     Pre-qualification. ERCOT must establish criteria for a large load customer to pre-
              qualify for participation in LLDMS. The criteria for pre-qualification must include
              the following minimum requirements:

       (1)   Request for proposal. ERCOT may issue a request for proposal to large load
            customers that are pre-qualified to participate in LLDMS for a procurement period
            of no more than seven days. Additional requests for proposals may be issued as
            needed. Requests for proposals under this subsection must be issued:

            (A)      based on monthly probabilistic modeling that identifies an elevated risk for
                     an EEA event in the modeled month;

            (B)      based on weekly weather forecasting that identifies an elevated risk for an
                     EEA event during the forecasted week;

            (C)      in advance of an anticipated Transmission Emergency, anticipated EEA
                     Level 1 event due to an extreme weather condition; or

            (D)      during a Transmission Emergency or an EEA event due to an extreme
                     weather condition.

      (2)   Quantity. The total quantity of MW that ERCOT procures for an LLDMS
            obligation period must be based on a risk assessment informed by probabilistic
            modeling.

      (3)   Submitted offer.

            (A)      Submission. A qualified scheduling entity (QSE) must submit an offer to
                     ERCOT on behalf of a large load customer that is pre-qualified to
                     participate in LLDMS. The offer must be expressed in dollars per megawatt
                     hour units.

            (B)      Rejection. ERCOT must reject an offer that is:

                     (i)     unreasonable;

                     (ii)    an outlier when evaluating the parameters of an acceptable offer;

                     (iii)   submitted on behalf of a large load customer that failed to comply
                             with ERCOT instructions to deploy during the previous LLDMS
                             obligation period;

                     (iv)    inconsistent with any other requirement established in ERCOT
                             protocols; or

                     (v)     greater than $5,000 per megawatt hour.

       (l)     ERCOT must establish criteria to reduce a QSE' s payment, claw back a QSE's
              payment, suspend a QSE from participation in LLDMS, reinstate a OSE's
              participation, or any combination thereof, based on the QSE's failure to meet its
              LLDMS obligation under this section or a related ERCOT protocol.

      (2)     ERCOT must establish criteria to suspend a large load customer based on
              noncompliance with this section or a related ERCOT protocol. ERCOT must also
              establish criteria for subsequent reinstatement.

      (3)     ERCOT must notify the commission of all alleged instances of noncompliance with
              this section or a related ERCOT protocol.

      (4)     ERCOT must maintain records relating to any alleged noncompliance with this
              section or a related ERCOT protocol.

(h)   After action reporting requirement. Not later than 60 days after an event in which
      ERCOT procures or deplovs LLDMS, ERCOT must file a report with the commission
      detailing:

      (1)     the number of large load customers that submitted offers;

      (2)     the number of megawatts procured;

      (3)     the highest offer;

      (4)     the lowest offer;

      (5)     the cleared price;

      (6)     the duration of deployment, as applicable;

      (7)     performance during deployment, as applicable; and

      (8)     any recommendation to revise LLDMS.

(i)   Implementation. ERCOT must develop, in consultation with commission staff, additional
      procedures, including registration requirements for the large load customers participating
      in LLDMS, guides, technical requirements, protocols. the order of deployment for
      LLDMS or other standards that are consistent with this section and that ERCOT finds
      necessary to develop LLDMS.
